power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Purpose: Formal and peer (informal) leaders play crucial roles in fostering team effectiveness and member well-being.
Although leadership research has examined a wide range of leader behaviors, it remains fragmented and typically focuses on either formal or peer leaders rather than both.
Moreover, no empirically grounded taxonomy captures the breadth of leadership behaviors across hierarchical levels.
Design/methodology/approach: To address this gap, we developed an inductively derived, literature-integrated taxonomy of leadership functions.
We first conducted qualitative interviews with 35 employees varying in hierarchical level, education, sector, and gender.
Qualitative content analysis identified leadership functions enacted by formal and peer leaders.
Participants then completed individual and group card-sorting exercises to cluster these functions into higher-order leadership roles.
Findings: The taxonomy comprised 10 formal and 10 peer leadership roles.
Comparison with existing leadership frameworks showed where prior research converges with and extends the leadership functions identified by participants.
Originality: This integrative taxonomy provides a practice-informed framework for advancing leadership theory and informing leadership development across organizational contexts.
Leadership is a key driver of individual, team, and organizational outcomes (Avolio et al., 2009; Sarros, 2011).

text.text: Over the past decades, leadership research has increasingly focused on leader behaviors, demonstrating their influence on a wide range of organizational outcomes (Judge et al., 2004; Piccolo et al., 2012).

text.text: Despite this progress, the field remains fragmented.

Leadership behaviors are often examined as isolated constructs or grouped into broad leadership styles, resulting in disconnected frameworks that hamper cumulative theory development (Banks et al., 2023; Cronin et al., 2021; Homan et al., 2020).

text.text: Consequently, the field lacks an empirically grounded taxonomy that integrates formal and peer leadership within a common behavioral framework.
This fragmentation reflects two conceptual challenges.
First, leadership is commonly conceptualized through broad styles or follower perceptions rather than the specific behaviors through which it is enacted.
Second, although leadership is increasingly recognized as emerging from both formal and peer leaders, these sources are typically studied separately.

Research has predominantly focused on formal leadership (Leino, 2022), whereas shared and informal leadership have rarely been examined alongside it within an integrated behavioral framework (Wang et al., 2014).

text.text: Consequently, it remains unclear which leadership behaviors are shared across formal and peer leaders, which are source-specific, and how they jointly shape leadership in teams.
To address these challenges, we developed an empirically grounded taxonomy of formal and peer leadership behaviors based on employees' perceptions.
Rather than identifying new behaviors, our contribution lies in integrating dispersed knowledge into a coherent leadership framework for everyday team practice.

We conducted qualitative interviews to identify behaviors associated with effective formal and peer leaders, organized them into distinct leadership roles using inductive and Classification: Internal deductive classification procedures, and compared the resulting taxonomy with existing leadership frameworks.
Our study contributes to leadership research in three ways.
First, it provides an empirically grounded taxonomy that integrates formal and peer leadership within a single conceptual framework, supporting programmatic theory development (Cronin et al., 2021).

text.text: Second, by shifting attention from broad leadership styles to concrete behaviors, it offers greater conceptual precision regarding how leadership is enacted in teams.

Third, by distinguishing shared from source-specific behaviors, the taxonomy provides a stronger foundation for future research on shared and multi-source leadership processes (D' Innocenzo et al., 2016; Edelmann et al., 2023).

Examining both sources therefore provides a more complete understanding of leadership in teams.

text.text: Despite growing recognition that leadership is distributed across multiple actors, behavioral taxonomies continue to focus primarily on formal leaders or treat leadership as a collective process.
Consequently, little is known about how formal and peer leadership behaviors compare and complement one another.

text.text: Research on team roles increasingly recognizes that leadership is not exclusively exercised by formal leaders but can emerge through interactions among team members.

This perspective is reflected in theories of shared, distributed, and collectivistic leadership, which conceptualize leadership as a dynamic influence process enacted by multiple actors rather than a single formal leader (Carson et al., 2007; Denis et al., 2012; Pearce and Conger, 2003; Yammarino et al., 2012).

text.text: Together, these perspectives position peer leadership as an emergent, relational phenomenon that contributes to team functioning.
Alongside this work, numerous frameworks have classified team roles.

Early models distinguished task and social roles (Bales, 1950 (Bales, , 1970;; Benne and Sheats, 1948), while later frameworks identified broader behavioral and functional roles within teams (Barry, 1991; Belbin, 1981 Belbin, , 1993;; Burke et al., 2018; Driskell et al., 2017; DuBrin, 1995; Lehmann-Willenbrock et al., 2016; Mathieu et al., 2015; Mumford et al., 2006; Stempfle et al., 2001).

To address these gaps, we conducted two complementary studies to develop parallel behavioral taxonomies for formal and peer leaders based on employees' accounts of leadership behaviors that support team functioning and employee well-being.

text.text: Study 2 used concept mapping to cluster the leadership functions identified in Study 1 into broader leadership roles.

Following established procedures (Wilkinson, 2004), experienced leadership practitioners first completed an individual cardsorting exercise, after which the resulting categorizations were discussed and refined in three Classification: Internal focus groups.

Participants.
Using convenience sampling, we recruited 12 experienced leadership practitioners (RR = 20.33%), including Learning and Development specialists, HR managers, business consultants, and team coaches.
All had extensive experience leading, coaching, or developing teams.
Concept mapping consisted of two phases.
First, participants individually sorted the 49 formal and 39 peer leadership functions from Study 1 into conceptually similar clusters.
Second, three focus groups reviewed and refined these categorizations to reach consensus on broader leadership roles.

Consistent with previous concept-mapping research (Morente-Molinera et al., 2021; Paul, 2008), functions were considered conceptually related when grouped together by at least two of the three focus groups (≥50% agreement).

text.text: Participants also rated the level of consensus using a 7-point agreement scale and a percentage estimate.
Participants reported a high level of perceived consensus (M = 5.6 on a 7-point scale, SD = 0.65), corresponding to an average agreement of 82.8%.
Of the 49 formal and 39 peer leadership functions, 12 and four, respectively, did not initially meet the predefined consensus threshold.

After reviewing the individual card-sorting results and focus group discussions, all but two functions -Seeking and being open to employee participation (formal leadership) and Taking responsibility and going beyond what is required (peer leadership) -were meaningfully assigned to an overarching leadership role.
As no clear consensus emerged, these functions were retained as stand-alone items.
Overall, the concept-mapping procedure yielded 10 formal and 10 peer leadership roles.
Role labels were assigned iteratively by the research team based on the content of the underlying functions.

To facilitate use across Classification: Internal organizational contexts, each role received both a leadership label (e.g., Motivational leader) and a neutral label (e.g., Motivator) (Tables II and III).

This study developed an empirically grounded taxonomy of leadership behaviors enacted by formal and peer leaders.
By clustering employees' descriptions of leadership behaviors into roles and comparing these with existing frameworks, we provide an integrated overview of leadership across hierarchical levels.
Our analyses identified 10 formal and 10 peer leadership roles.

Consistent with classic leadership research (e.g., Bales and Slater, 1955), the findings confirm the enduring importance of task-and relationship-oriented leadership while revealing a more differentiated behavioral repertoire within these broad categories.

text.text: Determining the relative impact of specific leadership roles requires future quantitative research.
Study 1 identified 49 formal leadership functions, which were clustered into 10 leadership roles in Study 2.
Together, these reflected both task-and relationship-oriented leadership, suggesting that employees value leaders who support team performance and employee well-being.

The most frequently mentioned functions were person-oriented, including paying attention to employees' work situations (89%), showing personal interest (69%), and fostering a positive team atmosphere through social activities during working hours (60%), consistent with growing attention to people-centered leadership approaches such as servant leadership.
Many identified roles align closely with established leadership frameworks.
For example, the Task Leader reflects traditional task-oriented behaviors, whereas the Connecting Leader and Motivational Leader emphasize relationships and employee well-being.
Comparison with existing frameworks (Tables IV and V) showed substantial overlap with Yukl (2012), Fleishman et al. (1991), and Morgeson et al. (2010).

In particular, the Proximity Leader and Social Activity Leader emphasize accessibility, vulnerability, social connection, and team cohesion, whereas the Self-development Leader highlights leaders' responsibility to continuously develop their leadership capabilities (Ashford and DeRue, 2012; Reichard et al., 2017).

text.text: These findings suggest that established leadership roles remain relevant while highlighting behaviors that have become increasingly important in contemporary work environments.

text.text: Study 1 identified 37 peer leadership functions, which were clustered into 10 leadership roles in Study 2.
Many roles align with existing frameworks on team roles and informal leadership.

For example, the Task Leader, Team-Development Leader, External Leader, and Connecting Leader correspond closely with previous taxonomies (e.g., Driskell et al., 2017; Fransen et al., 2014; Morgeson et al., 2010).

text.text: At the same time, the taxonomy identifies less-studied roles, including the Logistics Leader, Unity Leader, and Proximity Leader, suggesting that peer leadership extends beyond coordinating work to supporting the operational and social functioning of teams.

Participants also expected peer leaders to enact behaviors traditionally associated with formal leaders, including challenging the team, providing resources, supporting colleagues' development, and taking initiative.

Although this contrasts with Morgeson et al. (2010), it is consistent with increasingly autonomous and less hierarchical work environments in which leadership responsibilities are shared more broadly.

text.text: Finally, the Exemplary Leader and Unity Leader may represent cross-cutting roles that strengthen the enactment of other leadership roles through role modeling (i.e., leading by example; Bao et al., 2018; Coetzer et al., 2017; Kiker et al., 2019) and fostering a shared team identity (Fransen et al., 2020; Steffens et al., 2014).

text.text: Likewise, the stand-alone function taking responsibility and going beyond what is required may represent a broader behavioral quality that supports multiple leadership roles.
Comparing the formal and peer leadership taxonomies revealed substantial overlap.

Eight leadership roles -Task Leader, Connecting Leader, Social Activity Leader, Motivational Leader, Team-Development Leader, External Leader, Exemplary Leader, and Unity Leader -emerged across both leadership sources, supporting the view of leadership as a distributed process across hierarchical levels.

text.text: However, shared role labels did not necessarily reflect identical behaviors.

For example, whereas formal Motivational Leaders emphasized communicating the importance and progress of the team's work, peer Motivational Leaders primarily encouraged colleagues to speak up and take initiative.
These findings highlight the importance of interpreting leadership roles alongside their underlying behavioral functions.
Several roles were source-specific.
Proximity Leader, Unity Leader, and Selfdevelopment Leader emerged only for formal leaders, whereas Critical Innovation Leader and Logistics Leader were unique to peer leaders.
These differences likely reflect the distinct positions of formal and peer leaders within teams.

Formal leaders are expected to remain accessible and develop their leadership capabilities, whereas peer leaders are expected to take initiative, drive improvement, and provide day-to-day operational support (Harari et al., 2021; Jiang et al., 2021; Martínez-Córcoles and Zhu, 2020).

text.text: This difference may reflect the increasing autonomy and innovation demands of contemporary organizations, where employees are expected to take greater ownership of team functioning.

Overall, the taxonomy converged strongly with existing leadership frameworks while identifying less-studied roles, including the Proximity Leader, Logistics Leader, Social Activity Leader, and Unity Leader.
Although modest variation in the frequency of specific Classification: Internal leadership behaviors was observed across industries (Appendix C), the overall pattern was highly consistent.
This study advances leadership theory by offering a more behaviorally specific understanding of leadership in teams.

First, by adopting an inductive, data-driven approach, this study responds to calls to focus leadership research on observable behaviors rather than broad leadership styles or generalized perceptions (Banks et al., 2023).

text.text: Grounded in employees' descriptions of everyday leadership, the taxonomy provides greater behavioral specificity than many existing frameworks and a stronger foundation for future measurement development.

Although several roles overlap with established leadership theories (e.g., transformational, authentic, and servant leadership), these overlaps reflect the integration of complementary perspectives into a coherent behavioral taxonomy rather than conceptual fragmentation.
Second, the taxonomy conceptualizes leadership as concrete behaviors enacted by both formal and peer leaders rather than as a formal position or shared team property.
By distinguishing overlapping from source-specific roles, it provides a framework for understanding how different leadership sources jointly contribute to team functioning.
Third, the taxonomy contributes to shared leadership research by specifying which leadership roles are shared across formal and peer leaders and which remain source-specific.
This provides a more precise basis for examining how leadership responsibilities are distributed and how different leadership sources complement one another (D' Innocenzo et al., 2016).

text.text: In doing so, it moves beyond an either/or view of formal versus distributed leadership by demonstrating that effective team leadership comprises both overlapping and source-specific behaviors enacted by different leadership sources.

Finally, by consolidating dispersed leadership behaviors into an empirically grounded taxonomy spanning formal and peer leadership, this study provides a foundation for more programmatic theory development and measurement and offers a more unified framework for understanding team leadership (Cronin et al., 2021).

text.text: The proposed taxonomy offers practical guidance for formal leaders, teams, HR professionals, and organizations.

By distinguishing between formal and peer leadership roles, it clarifies which responsibilities should remain with formal leaders and which can be shared with team members, supporting more deliberate delegation and shared leadership.

It also provides a common language for diagnosing leadership gaps, overlap, and overload, informing leadership development, team interventions, onboarding, role clarification, performance conversations, and assessment (e.g., Shared Leadership Mapping; Fransen et al., 2020).

text.text: Our findings further show that both formal and peer leaders are expected to enact a broad repertoire of task-and relationship-oriented behaviors, highlighting the increasing complexity of formal leadership (Yukl, 2010) while creating opportunities to distribute leadership more effectively across team members, strengthening ownership and accountability for team outcomes (George, 1992; Williams et al., 1981).

text.text: A key strength of this study is its bottom-up qualitative design, which generated rich insights into leadership behaviors that are difficult to capture using surveys (Carton, 2022).

text.text: The stratified sample enhanced diversity across organizational contexts, while combining current and ideal leadership behaviors provided a comprehensive overview of employees' Classification: Internal leadership expectations.
Combining individual and group concept-mapping exercises further strengthened the taxonomy by integrating independent and collective judgments.
Although the qualitative concept-mapping approach generated rich insights, the taxonomy requires quantitative validation through scale development and confirmatory factor analysis.
Future research should also examine how leadership behaviors and configurations influence team functioning across leadership sources and organizational contexts.
A limitation of Study 2 is that participants assigned every leadership function to a role, making some conceptual overlap inevitable.
Future research should therefore examine the distinctiveness of the identified roles and the combinations most beneficial across contexts.

Social network analysis could examine whether multiple roles are enacted by the same or different individuals, whereas Necessary Condition Analysis (Dul, 2018) may identify leadership roles that are essential but not sufficient for effective team functioning.

text.text: Future research should examine how leadership functions evolve across team development and whether roles are most effective when enacted by formal leaders, peer leaders, or both.

Likewise, it remains unclear whether peer leadership is most effective when multiple leadership roles are concentrated in one individual or distributed across several team members (e.g., Fransen et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2018).

text.text: This study presents an empirically grounded taxonomy integrating formal and informal leadership behaviors into a cohesive framework, addressing fragmentation in the existing literature.
Our findings show that many leadership roles are shared across leadership sources, whereas others are unique to either formal or peer leaders, highlighting how leadership is distributed within teams.
By consolidating these roles, we offer a foundation for future research on leadership as a shared phenomenon involving both formal and peer leaders.
